The Ferry Inquiry Will Fail Unless We Ask a Duller Question
By Marta Okonjo-Reyes, columnist

Every disaster produces the same ritual. A minister promises a review, a review promises a report, and the report lands in a season when nobody is reading. I have watched this cycle four times in this city, and I am no longer willing to pretend the ritual is the same thing as accountability.

The Meridian Maritime Authority's preliminary summary is a serious document. It says the starboard generator failed and the backup did not engage. What it does not say, and what the ministry has avoided saying, is who decided that a nineteen-minute failure window was an acceptable risk on a route carrying two hundred people at a time.

That decision was not an accident. Somebody wrote an inspection interval into a schedule, somebody else approved it, and a budget line made it cheaper to keep the older vessels running. Ilse Vantorren, the authority's safety director, said the maintenance record is the center of the inquiry. She is right, but maintenance records describe what was done, not what was permitted.

I think the ministry will resist this framing, because it converts a technical failure into a political one. It is easier to fault a generator than a procurement committee. The transport ministry's own five-year plan, published in 2024, projected a fleet replacement that has not started.

None of this proves malice. It is entirely possible that every person in the chain acted reasonably given what they knew, and that the outcome was still indefensible. Both things can be true, and the inquiry should be built to find out which.

So ask the duller question. Not why the generator failed, but who signed the schedule that let it matter.
